To assemble a sample, RiboPilot compares its reads with known ribosomal
sequences from related organisms: a reference database. RiboPilot does not ship
one. You build one for each group of related samples, fishes included, and it is
reused by every later project on that group.

You do not need to find or format any sequences yourself, and in most projects
you do not need to run a command either: the app's **Reference** step does it for
you, using the taxonomy you assigned. This guide covers that step.

# The Reference step

The Reference step comes between the **Taxonomy** and **Assemble** steps. A
sample assembles with the database its **Assembly Options** name, and a new
project names a fish database that RiboPilot does not ship, so set up a database
for every group before you assemble.

Once your samples' taxonomy is assigned, open the Reference step and press
**Propose groups**. RiboPilot looks at each sample's lineage and groups samples
that can share one reference database, using how many ribosomal sequences
GenBank holds for each candidate group: a group needs at least 1,000 GenBank
records to make a useful reference, and RiboPilot picks the narrowest group
(family, order, class, and so on) that clears that bar. If that group holds more
than 25,000 records, the proposal says so in red: its database takes longer to
build, and you can narrow it later with **Change which clade this group uses**.
Samples from very different parts of the tree end up in different groups, each
with its own database.

Each row is one proposed group. The **Status** column says where that group
stands ("Needs a database", "Building", "Ready", "Build failed", or "Left on
current database"), and the rest of the row shows the clade, how many of your
samples it covers, and how many GenBank records back it up.

## Setting a group up

The link at the right-hand end of each row says what that group needs: **Set up
database**, **Try again**, or **Change**. Click it and you are offered four
choices:

- **Download sequences from GenBank.** The normal choice. Opens a run window, the
  same kind the Assemble step uses, showing the command that will run and letting
  you set an NCBI API key or restrict to RefSeq records first. Press **Run from
  App** and the download happens through RiboPilot's Nextflow workflow, with
  live progress in the window. Keep the browser tab open until the build
  finishes. Closing the tab or pressing **Stop / Interrupt** stops the build
  cleanly; press **Run from App** again with **Resume previous run?** ticked to
  carry on. If the app runs headless (see [Running on a cluster](Clusters.html)),
  the window offers a cluster job script to submit instead. When a build finishes,
  RiboPilot automatically points that group's samples at the new database and
  writes the files to your reference folder (see below). Samples already locked
  in the Assemble step are left alone, since their results were produced with
  whatever database they had before. A group whose database already exists on
  disk is wired up immediately, without starting a new build.
- **Use a database I already have.** Points the group at a database that was
  already built, either earlier in this project or by someone else sharing the
  same reference folder.
- **Change which clade this group uses.** Opens the group's shared lineage as a
  ladder, from the broadest rank down to the narrowest, each rung showing how
  many samples it covers and, for rungs RiboPilot has already counted, how many
  GenBank records back them up; an uncounted rung shows "records unknown" rather
  than triggering a new count. Pick a different rung to widen or narrow the
  group, or search for another clade entirely. If the rung you pick does not
  cover every sample in the group, the leftover samples are split off into a
  group of their own so nobody is left under the wrong reference. You can also
  reach this by clicking the group's **Clade** cell directly.
- **Leave these samples on their current database.** Nothing is built. Use it
  only when you have already pointed these samples' **Assembly Options** at a
  database yourself.

To handle several groups at once, tick their rows first, then click the link on
any one of them: the choice you make applies to the whole selection. The clade
option is offered only for a single group, since the ladder walks one group's
shared lineage.

If you press **Update** in the Assemble step while some groups have no database,
RiboPilot warns you but goes ahead: those samples assemble with whatever database
their **Assembly Options** name, as if you had left them on their current
database. For a new project that is the fish database RiboPilot does not ship,
so those samples fail.

# The reference folder

Built databases live in a **reference folder** that is shared across projects:
one clade database, built once, is reused by every project that needs that clade,
and if the folder is on a shared drive, by everyone in your lab. You can set it in
the Reference step with the **Settings** button (which also lets you adjust the
minimum and maximum record counts the grouping step uses), or when you create a
project:

```r
RiboPilot::new_project(
  path       = "~/my_project",
  mapping_fn = "~/my_samples.csv",
  data_path  = "~/my_reads",
  ref_dir    = "~/ribopilot_refs"
)
```

If you do not set a folder, RiboPilot uses a folder in your home directory;
`RiboPilot::ribopilot_ref_dir()` prints it. On a cluster, move it off your home
directory: see [Disk space, caches, and offline use](Caches-and-Offline.html).

You can also build a database from R; see
[Advanced: scripting RiboPilot](Scripting.html).

# Good to know

- **Build once, reuse forever.** From the Reference step, a group whose database
  already exists on disk is simply wired up without starting a new build.
- **Groups with few sequences.** Some groups have very little published ribosomal
  data. The Reference step handles this by walking up the lineage until it finds
  a clade with enough records, for example a whole family or order rather than a
  single genus.
- **The 5.8S gene.** GenBank rarely stores 5.8S on its own; it is usually bundled
  inside ITS records. That is fine: RiboPilot still recovers the 5.8S region from
  the full repeat, and its quality checks look at the 18S, 5.8S, and 28S genes.
